facts.statement: The genus Bothriolepis was described by Eichwald in 1840.
facts.quote: authority: Eichwald, 1840

facts.statement: Bothriolepis inhabited near-shore marine and freshwater environments across all paleocontinents.
facts.quote: Historically, Bothriolepis resided in an array of paleo-environments spread across every paleocontinent, including near shore marine and freshwater settings.

facts.statement: Most species of Bothriolepis were small, benthic freshwater detritivores averaging about 30 cm in length.
facts.quote: Most species of Bothriolepis were characterized as relatively small, benthic, freshwater detritivores (organisms that obtain nutrients by consuming decomposing plant/animal material), averaging around 30 cm in length.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis is classified within the placoderm order Antiarchi.
facts.quote: Bothriolepis is a genus placed within the placoderm order Antiarchi.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis is characterized by bony plates covering its head and the anterior part of its trunk.
facts.quote: Antiarchs, as well as other placoderms, are morphologically diverse and are characterized by bony plates that cover their head and the anterior part of the trunk.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis had a keyhole-shaped opening on the top of its head for eyes and nostrils and a mouth opening on the lower side near the front.
facts.quote: There are two openings through the head of Bothriolepis: a keyhole opening along the midline on the upper side for the eyes and nostrils and an opening for the mouth on the lower side near the anterior end of the head.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis possessed a preorbital recess, a bone partition below the eye and nostril openings that enclosed the nasal capsules.
facts.quote: It had a special feature on its skull, a separate partition of bone below the opening for the eyes and nostrils enclosing the nasal capsules called a preorbital recess.

facts.statement: In adults, Bothriolepis had two separate jaw halves that were functionally independent.
facts.quote: Bothriolepis has a jaw in which the two halves are separate and in the adult are functionally independent.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis likely had a slender trunk covered in soft skin without scales or markings.
facts.quote: Bothriolepis had a slender trunk that was likely covered in soft skin with no scales or markings.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis likely rested with its dorsal side up, supported by a flat ventral surface.
facts.quote: The orientation that appears to have been mostly stable for resting was the dorsal surface up, evidenced by the flat surface on the ventral side.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis had a box-like body enclosed in armor plates for predator protection.
facts.quote: Its box-like body was enclosed in armor plates, providing protection from predators.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Bothriolepis used its spike-like pectoral fins to lift its armored body off the bottom.
facts.quote: These spike-like fins were probably used to lift the body clear off the bottom; its heavy armor would have made it sink quickly as soon as it lost forward momentum.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis is now considered to have only a single high, rounded posterior dorsal fin.
facts.quote: In addition to the pectoral fins, it is originally considered to have two dorsal fins, but existence of a low, elongated anterior dorsal fin was denied in 1996, and now it is considered to have only a high rounded posterior dorsal fin.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis lacked pelvic fins.
facts.quote: Bothriolepis lacked pelvic fins.

facts.statement: Robert Denison published a paper exploring the soft anatomy and organs of Bothriolepis.
facts.quote: Robert Denison's paper titled "The Soft Anatomy of Bothriolepis" explores the forms and organs of Bothriolepis.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis possessed a specialized complex spiral valve in its digestive system, similar to that found in some sharks.
facts.quote: While the alimentary system is primitive in nature and lacks an expanded stomach region, it is specialized by an independently acquired complex spiral valve, comparable to that in elasmobranchs and many bony fish and similar to that found in some sharks.

facts.statement: It is unclear exactly when gnathostomes emerged, though the fossil record suggests the Early Palaeozoic era.
facts.quote: It is unclear exactly when gnathostomes emerged, but the scant early fossil record indicates that it was sometime in the Early Palaeozoic era.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Bothriolepis had a notochord, as the trunk outline suggests one but no direct evidence exists due to soft tissue decay.
facts.quote: The trunk's outline suggests that there may have been a notochord present surrounded by a membranous sheath, however, there is no direct evidence of this since the notochord is made up of soft tissue, which is not typically preserved in the fossil record.

facts.statement: Compared to normal fish, the gill region of Bothriolepis was positioned more dorsally, was anteriorly crowded, and was relatively short and broad.
facts.quote: Compared to the gills of normally-shaped fish, the gill region of Bothriolepis is considered to be placed more dorsally, is anteriorly more crowded, and in general is relatively short and broad.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the ventral sacs of Bothriolepis functioned as lungs that allowed the animal to travel on land.
facts.quote: It has been hypothesized that these lungs, coupled with the jointed arms and rigid, supportive skeleton, would have allowed Bothriolepis to travel on land.

facts.statement: Not all paleontologists agree with the 1941 interpretation that Bothriolepis possessed lungs.
facts.quote: Despite the original interpretation presented by Denison in 1941, not all paleontologists agree that placoderms like Bothriolepis actually possessed lungs.

facts.statement: Some researchers believe the presence of lungs in Bothriolepis is uncertain because its fossils are found in strictly marine environments.
facts.quote: He notes that the worldwide distribution of Bothriolepis is restricted to strictly marine environments, and thus believes that the presence of lungs in Bothriolepis is uncertain.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis fed by swallowing mouthfuls of mud and soft sediments to digest detritus, microorganisms, algae, and organic matter.
facts.quote: Bothriolepis, as with all other antiarchs, are thought to have fed by directly swallowing mouthfuls of mud and other soft sediments in order to digest detritus, small or microorganisms, algae, and other forms of organic matter in the swallowed sediments.

facts.statement: The ventral positioning of the mouth suggests that Bothriolepis was a bottom-feeder.
facts.quote: Additionally, the positioning of the mouth on the ventral side of its head further suggests that Bothriolepis was likely a bottom-feeder.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis fossils are found in strata dating from 387 to 360 million years ago.
facts.quote: Bothriolepis fossils are found in Middle and Late Devonian strata (from 387 to 360 million years ago).

facts.statement: Bothriolepis fossils have been found in Asia, Europe, Australia, Africa, North America, and South America.
facts.quote: Large groupings of Bothriolepis specimens have been found in Asia, Europe, Australia (Gogo Formation and Mandagery Sandstone), Africa (Waterloo Farm lagerstätte) Pennsylvania (Catskill Formation), Quebec (Escuminac Formation), Virginia (Chemung), Colorado, Cuche Formation (Boyacá, Colombia), and all around the world.

facts.statement: More than two hundred individuals of Bothriolepis were found packed closely together at the Catskill Formation site.
facts.quote: More than two hundred individuals were found packed closely together with little to no overlap.

facts.statement: The species B. nitida and B. minor were described from the Catskill Formation site.
facts.quote: B. nitida and B. minor are also described from this site.

facts.statement: Bothriolepis canadensis was first described in 1880 by J.F. Whiteaves.
facts.quote: B. canadensis was first described in 1880 by J.F. Whiteaves, using a limited number of disfigured samples.

facts.statement: E. Stensio published a widely accepted detailed depiction of B. canadensis anatomy in 1948.
facts.quote: In 1948, E. Stensio released a detailed depiction of B. canadensis anatomy using an abundance of material, which eventually became the most widely accepted description of this species.

facts.statement: Remains of B. africana have been recovered exclusively from the Witpoort Formation near Makhanda/Grahamstown in South Africa.
facts.quote: Remains have exclusively been recovered from a single carbonaceous shale near the top of the Late Devonian, Famennian, Witpoort Formation (Witteberg Group) exposed in a road cutting south of Makhanda/Grahamstown in South Africa.

facts.statement: The head and trunk armor of B. africana ranged from 20 to 300 mm, corresponding to full body lengths between 52 and 780 mm.
facts.quote: The head and trunk armour lengths ranged between 20 - 300 mm which translates, based on the proportions of two of the smallest individuals (in which tail impressions are preserved) into full body lengths varying between 52 - 780 mm.

facts.statement: B. coloradensis was first described by Eastman in 1904 and found in present-day Colorado.
facts.quote: First described by Eastman in 1904, this species was found localized in present-day Colorado.

facts.statement: It is debated whether B. coloradensis is similar to or identical to B. nitida due to the fragmented nature of the available material.
facts.quote: There is a possibility that this species is similar, if not identical, to B. nitida, however because the material available regarding B. coloradensis is fragmented, it is impossible to compare the two species with any degree of certainty.
